doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

chapter: Swing Street shows and the business
title: Jazz parties versus festivals
summary: He prefers jazz parties but notes the limited repertoire when players do not prepare sets.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Do you enjoy playing these jazz parties? You get to invite all the different musicians?

Yeah. I like the jazz parties as opposed to the jazz festivals where they have organized bands. Yes, the parties are wonderful where they invite anywhere from 15 to 30 musicians, three or four on each instrument and they put you together different combinations. Some of them are good, some of them are not so good, it depends on the attitude of the players that go to some of them. Some are very self — don’t want to budge too much and therefore the repertoire ends up being more limited than it could be. In other words it will come down to maybe one of two hundred tunes that everybody knows. And you get tired of playing “Undecided” and “Jumpin’ at the Woodside” and a few of the other tunes, and “One O’Clock Jump” or, you know, “Don’t Get Around Much Anymore” or “Satin Doll.” I mean they’re all great tunes but you get there and you’ve got six guys, okay now what are we going to do guys? If the leader on a given set really puts in some time ahead of time and says okay I’ve got a great swing set here or I’ve have a very traditional set, let’s do a traditional set, and so it depends how much time you put in © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
on it and some guys don’t, some of the players just go and they’re kind of lackadaisical about it. So some of the festivals are good, some of them aren’t. It’s not all wonderful.
